about: Read with: passages the editors pair because one echoes, imitates, answers, sources or contrasts with the other. Each side names one text in one translation (ref) and its lines as this archive counts them (l), or its paragraphs in a prose translation (p); in Murray's Homer, l is the Greek line numbers. og gives the original's book and lines, so the pair also shows in every translation of that book. Notes are the editors' own, drafted from the study notes and public-domain commentaries; no modern criticism is quoted. Made by work/featuretest/echo/build.py.

a.label: Iliad 1.1–7 (Murray)
first: The wrath sing, goddess, of Peleus' son, Achilles, that destructive wrath which brought countless woes upon the Achaeans, and sent forth to Hades many valiant souls of…

b.label: Aeneid 1.1–11 (Dryden)
first: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate,
And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate,

pairs.note: Homer asks the goddess to sing a wrath; Virgil says 'I sing' of arms and a man, and only then turns to the Muse for causes. The Aeneid opens by naming both Homeric poems at once (arms for the Iliad, the man for the Odyssey) and by putting the poet's own voice first.
pairs.q: What changes when the poet says 'I sing' instead of asking the Muse to sing?

b.label: Paradise Lost 1.1–26
first: Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast

pairs.note: Milton keeps the epic order (subject, then the call to the Muse, then a question about causes) but his subject is 'Man's first disobedience', and his Muse is the spirit that taught Moses on Sinai. He says outright that he means to soar above the classical poets: 'things unattempted yet in prose or rhyme'.
pairs.q: Milton promises to go beyond Homer and Virgil in the very form he borrows from them. Is that a contradiction?

a.label: Odyssey 1.1–10 (Murray)
first: Tell me, O Muse, of the man of many devices, who wandered full many ways after he had sacked the sacred citadel of Troy. Many were the men whose cities he saw and whose…

b.label: Aeneid 1.1–11 (Dryden)
first: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate,
And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate,

pairs.note: The Odyssey begins with 'the man' (andra) who wandered after Troy; the Aeneid's 'virum' answers it, but Virgil's man wanders toward a city still to be founded rather than back to a home. Both proems sum up a whole voyage in a few lines.
pairs.q: Odysseus travels home; Aeneas travels to a place he has never seen. How do the two openings prepare for that difference?

a.label: Aeneid 1.11 (Dryden)
first: Can heav’nly minds such high resentment show,
Or exercise their spite in human woe?

b.label: Paradise Lost 6.788
first: In heav'nly Spirits could such perverseness dwell?

pairs.note: Virgil's question 'tantaene animis caelestibus irae?' ('can heavenly minds hold such anger?') is turned by Milton into a line about the rebel angels: 'In heav'nly Spirits could such perverseness dwell?' Milton keeps the shape of the question but moves the blame from a goddess to fallen spirits.
pairs.q: Virgil asks the question about a goddess, Milton about rebels. Does the line mean the same thing in both places?

first: An airy crowd came rushing where he stood,

pairs.note: Glaucus tells Diomedes that the generations of men are like leaves, scattered by the wind and grown again in spring. pairs.q: Homer's leaves grow again; Virgil's only fall. What has changed in the meaning of the image?

pairs.note: Dante, guided by Virgil himself, rewrites Virgil's simile at the same river: the damned drop from the bank one by one 'as in the autumn-time the leaves fall off', and come at a signal 'as a bird unto its lure'. b.label: Inferno 3.82–99 (Longfellow)

pairs.note: Virgil's Charon is a filthy old ferryman with eyes of flame, a god still vigorous in age. Dante takes him over almost feature for feature, the white hair and the eyes ringed with fire, and lets him refuse a living passenger until Virgil speaks the formula that silences him.
pairs.q: Dante's Virgil commands Charon. What does it mean for Virgil's own creature to obey Virgil?
